extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature, philosophy, and moral reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of prescriptive principles and reflective guidance from Montaigne's essay (personal/philosophical prose). Useful for literary analysis or moral/philosophical study of Renaissance essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a just mean; follow Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “Servare modum, finemque tenere, Naturamque sequi.” — advocate for keeping a just mean, observing a just limit, and following Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valorize moderation and naturalness over elevation, pomp, or learned artificiality; prefer what serves the use of life rather than vain, idle fancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy and uniform greatness of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for a character 'always one and the same' who raises himself by temperament rather than starts or affectation (illustrated by Cato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer steady, sustained vigor and ordinary conduct in life and death rather than theatrical or sporadic heroics; solidity and regular motion convince and support the mind more than sharp affectations that merely ravish the judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness over learned pomp
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's design: to furnish precepts and things that 'more really and fitly serve to the use of life' rather than elevated display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ideas, writings, and actions by their service to everyday life and moral practice, not by their rhetorical elevation or ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about intellectual excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that curiosity and study carry vanity and weakness: 'We carry intemperance into the study of literature, as well as into everything else.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreaching in study; recognise that excessive learning can burden, alarm, or even poison the soul; prefer modest, necessary knowledge to speculative excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vow of mental poverty (humility of mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commends those who, alongside vows of chastity/poverty/penitence, vow ignorance — to geld unruly appetites and blunt cupidity for books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate intellectual humility; deliberately limit the appetite for knowledge when it becomes voluptuous or distracts from living well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books as exercise and potential distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Books have not so much served for instruction as exercise; they may imprint weight in imagination rather than fortify courage or true consolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use books as training, not as substitutes for lived courage; beware that some writings beautify or alarm more than they strengthen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish substance from style
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not call that force which is only a pretty knack of writing, nor that solid which is only sharp; 'everything that pleases does not nourish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically separate rhetorical brilliance or stylistic niceties from real strength and moral or intellectual substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from unlearned people's natural constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe how peasants and common people, ignorant of philosophers, exhibit genuine constancy, patience, and courage; names soften disease and they endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that nature and ordinary practice often provide truer models of virtue than learned systems — value examples from plain life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid violent cures for social ills
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject remedies like civil war or destroying government to 'cure' a political disease — Plato's and Favonius' caution against violent reformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer preservation, prudence, and lawful patience to radical, violent upheaval that risks citizens' lives and the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of false religion as cloak for wickedness
rubrics_metrics.description: False religion is 'nothing has a more deceiving face' when crimes wear the cloak of virtue; the extremest injustice is reputed as just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to rhetoric of piety used to justify immoral acts; moral evaluation must look past professed motives to actual consequences and means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reliance in necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When friendship is rare, it is safest to trust oneself in necessity; 'true liberty is to be able to do what a man will with himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate resources and self-mastery so that, when fortune fails and external supports vanish, one can rely on one's own faculties and prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adversity as discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Ill scholars are admonished with the rod; adversity can be profitable to harden and fit life for new states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and use misfortune as practical exercise to prepare for worse; intentionally discipline desires and dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not anticipate evils to the point of misery
rubrics_metrics.description: Meditating exhaustively upon possible evils often troubles men as much as actual suffering: 'It troubles men as much that they may possibly suffer, as if they really did suffer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice measured foresight: prepare for dangers without letting the anticipation steal present peace; avoid making present life miserable out of fear of possible future harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable preparation, avoid morbid curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy ordains to have death before our eyes but also gives rules so this foresight harms not; physicians throw into diseases to use their art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for death and disaster in a way that is proportionate and preserves life’s continuity; do not cultivate morbid curiosity or speculative alarm that weakens rather than strengthens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature as corrective to sophistic reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We have 'sophisticated' nature with far-fetched discourses so she became variable; we must sometimes learn from beasts and simple life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reason becomes excessively subtle or corruptible, return to natural, simple examples and instincts to recover universal, constant moral bearings.
